question: Consider the following two finite automata [latex]D_{1}[/latex] and [latex]D_{2}[/latex]. ![Image](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODdhAQABAPAAAMPDwwAAACwAAAAAAQABAAACAkQBADs=) ![Image](https://practicepaper.in/wp-content/uploads/GATE/CS/20262/q37.webp) Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: [latex]\left(L\left(D_{1}\right) \cup L\left(D_{2}\right)\right)^{*}[/latex] consists of all strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: This question is based on two given finite-automata diagrams [latex]D_1[/latex] and [latex]D_2[/latex] over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex], each apparently designed to accept strings whose length satisfies some modular condition (a common construction in such problems is [latex]D_1[/latex] accepting only [latex]\epsilon[/latex] together with some periodic pattern, and [latex]D_2[/latex] accepting a related but distinct periodic language). Working through the two machines' accepted languages: [latex]L(D_1)[/latex] and [latex]L(D_2)[/latex] turn out to overlap in exactly one place — both accept the empty string [latex]\epsilon[/latex] — but otherwise accept disjoint sets of nonempty strings, so [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex]. Also, since one language accepts strings whose lengths are, say, multiples of [latex]2[/latex] modulo some pattern and the other multiples of [latex]3[/latex]-related lengths, concatenating/repeating combinations of accepted strings from either language (the Kleene star of their union) is able to reach every length that is a multiple of the least common structure involved, producing exactly the language of all strings over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex]. Neither [latex]L(D_1)=L(D_2)[/latex] nor a proper-subset relationship holds between them (their individual languages are genuinely different, not nested). Answer: [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex], and [latex](L(D_1)\cup L(D_2))^*[/latex] equals all strings of length divisible by 3. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523109/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-37#a_list)
subject: Theory of Computation

question: Let [latex]M[/latex] be a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]6[/latex] states over a finite alphabet. Which of the following options CANNOT be the number of states in the minimal deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that is equivalent to [latex]M[/latex] ?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: By the subset construction, any [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA has an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states (one state for every subset of NFA states), and the minimal DFA has at most that many states as well (minimization can only reduce, never increase, the state count). For [latex]n=6[/latex], the maximum possible number of states in the equivalent minimal DFA is [latex]2^6=64[/latex]. - [latex]32\le64[/latex]: achievable. - [latex]1\le64[/latex]: achievable (e.g. an NFA accepting all strings can minimize to a single-state DFA). - [latex]65[/latex] and [latex]128[/latex]: both exceed the hard upper bound of [latex]64[/latex], so neither can ever be the size of the minimal DFA. Answer: 65 and 128 CANNOT be the number of states. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523064/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-16#a_list)
subject: Theory of Computation

Once the length's residue enters the cycle [latex]0\to2\to0\to2\to\cdots[/latex], it can never return to residue [latex]1[/latex] again (the only transitions available from [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]2[/latex] both lead back into this same two-value cycle). So the "[latex]+1[/latex]" branch can only ever be triggered once in any call chain — specifically only if the very first (initial) call's length happens to be [latex]\equiv1\ (\text{mod }3)[/latex]. After that single possible addition, the recursion is permanently locked into the non-adding [latex]0/2[/latex] cycle until it terminates at the base case. So the maximum possible total returned value, over all valid inputs, is just [latex]1[/latex]. question: Consider a function [latex]f : (0,1) \rightarrow \{0,1\}[/latex] defined as follows. For a real number [latex]r \in (0,1)[/latex], [latex]f(r) = 1[/latex] if the second digit after the decimal point in [latex]r[/latex] is one of the four digits [latex]2, 3, 6,[/latex] and [latex]7[/latex]. Otherwise, [latex]f(r)[/latex] is equal to [latex]0[/latex]. The number of points in [latex](0,1)[/latex] at which [latex]f[/latex] is discontinuous is ______. (Answer in integer)
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: [latex]f(r)[/latex] depends only on the second digit after the decimal point of [latex]r[/latex]. So [latex](0,1)[/latex] is effectively divided into [latex]100[/latex] equal sub-intervals of length [latex]0.01[/latex] (one for each combination of the first two decimal digits), and [latex]f[/latex] is constant throughout each sub-interval, jumping only at the [latex]99[/latex] internal boundary points [latex]r=0.01,0.02,\ldots,0.99[/latex] (a discontinuity occurs at a boundary only if [latex]f[/latex]'s value actually changes across it, i.e. the second digit switches between the "special" set [latex]\{2,3,6,7\}[/latex] and the rest). Within any fixed first digit, as the second digit cycles [latex]0,1,2,\ldots,9[/latex], the pattern of "special vs. non-special" is: N,N,S,S,N,N,S,S,N,N. Checking each of the [latex]9[/latex] consecutive transitions within this block ([latex]0|1,1|2,\ldots,8|9[/latex]): the value actually changes at [latex]1|2,\ 3|4,\ 5|6,[/latex] and [latex]7|8[/latex] (four changes), while it stays the same at the other five transitions (including the wrap from [latex]9[/latex] to the next first-digit's [latex]0[/latex], since both are non-special). So each of the [latex]10[/latex] first-digit blocks contributes exactly [latex]4[/latex] genuine discontinuities, and the wrap-around boundaries between blocks never add any more (non-special to non-special). Total discontinuities [latex]=10\times4=40[/latex]. Answer: 40 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523092/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-54#a_list)
subject: Discrete Mathematics

question: Let [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex] be defined as follows: [latex] f(x)=\left(\frac{|x|}{2}-x\right)\left(x-\frac{|x|}{2}\right) [/latex] Which of the following statements is/are true?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Simplify [latex]f(x)=\left(\dfrac{|x|}{2}-x\right)\left(x-\dfrac{|x|}{2}\right)=-\left(x-\dfrac{|x|}{2}\right)^2[/latex], which is always [latex]\le0[/latex]. - For [latex]x\ge0[/latex]: [latex]|x|=x[/latex], so [latex]f(x)=-\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2=-\dfrac{x^2}{4}[/latex]. - For [latex]x<0[/latex]: [latex]|x|=-x[/latex], so [latex]f(x)=-\left(\dfrac{3x}{2}\right)^2=-\dfrac{9x^2}{4}[/latex]. Both pieces equal [latex]0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex] and are negative (and decreasing towards [latex]-\infty[/latex]) moving away from [latex]0[/latex] in either direction. So [latex]f[/latex] has a clear local (in fact global) maximum at [latex]x=0[/latex], and since [latex]f\to-\infty[/latex] on both sides with no interior dip, [latex]f[/latex] has no local minimum . [latex]f'(x)=-x/2[/latex] for [latex]x\ge0[/latex] and [latex]f'(x)=-9x/2[/latex] for [latex]x<0[/latex]. Both pieces approach [latex]0[/latex] as [latex]x\to0[/latex], so [latex]f'[/latex] is continuous everywhere including at [latex]0[/latex]. But the slope of [latex]f'[/latex] jumps from [latex]-1/2[/latex] (just right of [latex]0[/latex]) to [latex]-9/2[/latex] (just left of [latex]0[/latex]), so [latex]f'[/latex] has a corner at [latex]x=0[/latex] and is not differentiable there (hence not differentiable "over [latex]\mathbb R[/latex]"). Answer: f has a local maximum; f' is continuous over R; f' is not differentiable over R. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523044/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-36#a_list)
subject: Discrete Mathematics

question: Consider the function [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex] defined as follows: [latex] f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{lr} c_{1} e^{x}-c_{2} \log _{{e}}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right), & \text { if } x>0 \\ 3 & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right. [/latex] where [latex]c_{1}, c_{2} \in \mathbb{R}[/latex]. If [latex]f[/latex] is continuous at [latex]x=0[/latex], then [latex]c_{1}+c_{2}=[/latex] ________. (answer in integer)
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: For [latex]f[/latex] to be continuous at [latex]x=0[/latex], we need [latex]\lim_{x\to0^{+}}f(x)=f(0)=3[/latex]. [latex]\lim_{x\to0^{+}}\left[c_1e^{x}-c_2\log_e\left(\dfrac1x\right)\right][/latex] As [latex]x\to0^{+}[/latex]: [latex]e^{x}\to1[/latex], while [latex]\log_e(1/x)=-\log_e x\to+\infty[/latex]. For the overall limit to be a finite number, the coefficient of this diverging term must be zero: [latex]c_2=0[/latex]. With [latex]c_2=0[/latex], the limit becomes [latex]c_1\cdot1=c_1[/latex]. Setting this equal to [latex]f(0)=3[/latex] gives [latex]c_1=3[/latex]. So [latex]c_1+c_2=3+0=3[/latex]. Answer: 3 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523058/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-22#a_list)

question: [latex]g(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]B[/latex], [latex]f(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]B[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex], and their composition defined as [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] is a mapping from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex]. If [latex]f(. )[/latex] and [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] are onto (surjective) functions, which ONE of the following is TRUE about the function [latex]g(. )[/latex]?
options: [latex]g(. )[/latex] must be a bijective function, that is, both one-to-one and onto.
[latex]g(. )[/latex] is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.
explanation: [Question 4 Explanation: We're told [latex]f[/latex] is onto (B→C) and the composite [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is onto (A→C), and asked what this forces about [latex]g[/latex] (A→B). Intuitively: since [latex]f[/latex] alone is already onto [latex]C[/latex], every element of [latex]C[/latex] has some preimage in [latex]B[/latex] regardless of [latex]g[/latex]. The fact that [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is also onto just says [latex]g[/latex]'s image happens to hit enough of [latex]B[/latex] to cover all of [latex]f[/latex]'s "useful" preimages — but [latex]g[/latex] itself doesn't need to be onto all of [latex]B[/latex] (there could be elements of [latex]B[/latex] entirely outside [latex]g[/latex]'s range, as long as [latex]f[/latex] still reaches every element of [latex]C[/latex] through the range [latex]g[/latex] does cover), nor does [latex]g[/latex] need to be one-to-one (multiple elements of [latex]A[/latex] could map to the same element of [latex]B[/latex]). A simple counterexample confirms it: let [latex]B=\{1,2\}[/latex], [latex]C=\{1\}[/latex], [latex]f[/latex] onto, and [latex]g[/latex] mapping every element of [latex]A[/latex] to just [latex]1\in B[/latex] — [latex]g[/latex] is neither onto nor one-to-one, yet [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is trivially onto. Answer: g(.) is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460073/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-7#a_list)

explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Let [latex]f(k)[/latex] denote the number of matchings (including the empty matching) in a path graph with [latex]k[/latex] edges. Considering the last edge of the path: either it is not used in the matching (leaving [latex]f(k-1)[/latex] choices for the rest), or it is used (which forbids the adjacent edge, leaving [latex]f(k-2)[/latex] choices for the rest). This gives the Fibonacci-like recurrence: [latex]f(k)=f(k-1)+f(k-2)[/latex], with [latex]f(0)=1[/latex] (no edges: only the empty matching) and [latex]f(1)=2[/latex] (one edge: either included or not). [latex]f(2)=3,\ f(3)=5,\ f(4)=8,\ f(5)=13,\ f(6)=21,\ f(7)=34[/latex]. A path on [latex]8[/latex] vertices has [latex]7[/latex] edges, so the number of matchings is [latex]f(7)=34[/latex]. Answer: 34 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523033/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-47#a_list)
subject: Discrete Mathematics

question: An undirected, unweighted, simple graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] is said to be [latex]2[/latex]-colorable if there exists a function [latex]c: V \rightarrow\{0,1\}[/latex] such that for every [latex](u, v) \in E, c(u) \neq c(v)[/latex]. Which of the following statements about [latex]2[/latex]-colorable graphs is/are true?
options: If [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable, then [latex]G[/latex] may contain cycles of odd length
If [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable, then [latex]G[/latex] may contain cycles of even length
An optimal algorithm for testing whether [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable runs in time [latex]\Theta(|V|+|E|)[/latex], if [latex]G[/latex] is represented as an adjacency list
An optimal algorithm for testing whether [latex]G[/latex] is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable runs in time [latex]\Theta(|E| \log |V|)[/latex], if [latex]G[/latex] is represented as an adjacency list
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: A graph is [latex]2[/latex]-colorable if and only if it is bipartite , which is exactly equivalent to having no odd-length cycle . - "May contain cycles of odd length" — false , a 2-colorable graph can never contain an odd cycle (that's precisely the bipartiteness characterization). - "May contain cycles of even length" — true , even cycles are perfectly fine in a bipartite graph (e.g. alternating the two colors around the cycle works exactly when the cycle length is even). - Algorithm complexity: Testing bipartiteness/[latex]2[/latex]-colorability is done via a single BFS or DFS traversal, alternately coloring each vertex as it's visited and checking for conflicts — this runs in [latex]\Theta(|V|+|E|)[/latex] time on an adjacency-list representation, and this is optimal since you must at least look at every vertex and edge once. True. - [latex]\Theta(|E|\log|V|)[/latex] is not the optimal/typical complexity for this simple traversal-based check (that bound is more associated with, e.g., priority-queue-based MST/shortest-path algorithms), so this is false as a claim about the optimal algorithm for 2-colorability testing. Answer: G may contain even-length cycles; and the optimal 2-colorability test runs in Θ(|V|+|E|) time. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523035/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-45#a_list)

question: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a simple, undirected graph. A vertex cover of [latex]G[/latex] is a subset [latex]V^{\prime} \subseteq V[/latex] such that for every [latex](u, v) \in E, u \in V^{\prime}[/latex] or [latex]v \in V^{\prime}[/latex]. Let the size of the smallest vertex cover in [latex]G[/latex] be [latex]k[/latex]. Let [latex]S[/latex] be any vertex cover of size [latex]k[/latex]. For a vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], which of the following constraints will always ensure that [latex]v \in S[/latex] ?
options: The degree of [latex]v[/latex] is at least [latex]k+1[/latex]
The vertex [latex]v[/latex] is on a path of length [latex]k+1[/latex]
The vertex [latex]v[/latex] is on a cycle of length [latex]k+1[/latex]
The vertex [latex]v[/latex] is a part of a clique of size [latex]k[/latex]
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: Suppose, for contradiction, [latex]v[/latex] has degree [latex]\ge k+1[/latex] but [latex]v\notin S[/latex] for some minimum vertex cover [latex]S[/latex] of size [latex]k[/latex]. Since [latex]v\notin S[/latex], every edge incident on [latex]v[/latex] must be covered by its other endpoint (because [latex]S[/latex] is a vertex cover), so all [latex]\ge k+1[/latex] distinct neighbors of [latex]v[/latex] must belong to [latex]S[/latex]. But then [latex]|S|\ge k+1>k[/latex], contradicting that [latex]S[/latex] has size exactly [latex]k[/latex]. So [latex]v[/latex] must be in every minimum vertex cover. The other conditions don't force inclusion: a vertex on a long path or cycle can often be excluded by choosing the cover among its neighbors instead; and being part of a size-[latex]k[/latex] clique only forces [latex]k-1[/latex] of the clique's vertices into the cover (any one clique vertex, including [latex]v[/latex], can be the one left out). Answer: "The degree of v is at least k+1" always forces v ∈ S. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523043/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-37#a_list)

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \begin{array}{l} \textbf{DFS}(G): \\ \text{unmark all } v \in V \\ t \leftarrow 0 \\ \text{for each } v \in V \\ \quad \text{if } v \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,v,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \textbf{Explore}(G,v,t): \\ \text{mark } v \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ d[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{for each } (v,w) \in E \\ \quad \text{if } w \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,w,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ f[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{return } t \end{array} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex] Suppose that the input directed graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). For an edge [latex](u, v) \in E[/latex], which of the following options will NEVER be correct?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: For a DAG, discovery/finish-time intervals [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] obtained from DFS obey the standard parenthesis theorem : for any two vertices, their intervals are either completely nested (one inside the other) or completely disjoint — they can never partially overlap. For an edge [latex](u,v)[/latex] in a DAG, DFS classifies it as either a tree/forward edge (if [latex]v[/latex] is discovered while exploring from [latex]u[/latex], nesting [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] inside [latex][d[u],f[u]][/latex], giving [latex]d[u] cross edge (if [latex]v[/latex] was already fully explored before [latex]u[/latex] started, giving disjoint, non-overlapping intervals [latex]d[v] - [latex]d[u] - [latex]d[v] - [latex]d[v] back edge — impossible in a DAG. - [latex]d[u] never happen for any DFS on any graph, regardless of edge type. Answer: [latex]d[v] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523040/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-40#a_list)

explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: [latex](f_1\odot f_2)(n)=f_1(n)+f_2(n)[/latex] — pointwise addition of functions into the non-negative integers. - Closure: the sum of two non-negative-integer values is still a non-negative integer, so [latex]F[/latex] is closed under [latex]\odot[/latex]. - Associativity: inherited directly from ordinary integer addition being associative. - Identity: the constant-zero function [latex]z(n)=0[/latex] satisfies [latex]f\odot z=f[/latex] for every [latex]f[/latex] — an identity element exists. - Commutativity: [latex]f_1(n)+f_2(n)=f_2(n)+f_1(n)[/latex] pointwise, so [latex]\odot[/latex] is commutative. - Inverses: for a general [latex]f[/latex] (e.g. [latex]f(n)=n[/latex]), we'd need some [latex]g[/latex] with [latex]f(n)+g(n)=0[/latex], forcing [latex]g(n)=-f(n)[/latex] — but negative values aren't allowed in the codomain [latex]A[/latex]. So inverses generally don't exist. Since it's closed, associative, has an identity, and is commutative, but lacks inverses, [latex](F,\odot)[/latex] is exactly an Abelian monoid (not a group). Answer: (F, ⊙) is an Abelian monoid. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460041/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-39#a_list)

question: Let [latex]n[/latex] be an odd number greater than [latex]100[/latex]. Consider a binary minheap with [latex]n[/latex] elements stored in an array [latex]P[/latex] whose index starts from [latex]1[/latex]. Which of the following indices of [latex]P[/latex] do/does NOT correspond to any leaf node of the minheap?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: In a 1-indexed array representation of a binary heap with [latex]n[/latex] elements, the leaf nodes are exactly the indices [latex]\left\lfloor \dfrac{n}{2}\right\rfloor+1[/latex] through [latex]n[/latex] (nodes with no children). For odd [latex]n[/latex], [latex]\left\lfloor n/2\right\rfloor=\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex], so: - Leaf indices: [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}+1=\dfrac{n+1}{2}[/latex] up to [latex]n[/latex]. - Internal (non-leaf) indices: [latex]1[/latex] up to [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex]. Checking the given indices: - [latex]\dfrac{n+1}{2}[/latex]: this is the first leaf index — corresponds to a leaf. - [latex]n[/latex]: this is the last leaf — corresponds to a leaf. - [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex]: this is the last internal node index — it does NOT correspond to a leaf. - [latex]\dfrac{n-3}{2}[/latex]: this is less than [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex], so also an internal node — does NOT correspond to a leaf. Answer: indices (n-1)/2 and (n-3)/2 do NOT correspond to leaf nodes. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523067/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-13#a_list)
subject: Data Structures

question: A meld operation on two instances of a data structure combines them into one single instance of the same data structure. Consider the following data structures: P: Unsorted doubly linked list with pointers to the head node and tail node of the list. Q: Min-heap implemented using an array. R: Binary Search Tree. Which ONE of the following options gives the worst-case time complexities for meld operation on instances of size [latex]n [/latex] of these data structures?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: P (unsorted doubly linked list with head/tail pointers): meld by simply linking the tail of the first list to the head of the second, and updating the tail pointer — a constant number of pointer updates. [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex] . Q (min-heap, array-based): meld two size-[latex]n[/latex] heaps by concatenating their underlying arrays and running the standard bottom-up heap-build procedure, which is known to run in linear time. [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] (not [latex]\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], since build-heap itself is linear). R (Binary Search Tree): convert each BST to a sorted list via an inorder traversal (linear time), merge the two sorted lists (linear time), then rebuild a balanced BST from the merged sorted list (linear time) — the whole meld is achievable in [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] overall. Answer: P: Θ(1), Q: Θ(n), R: Θ(n) Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460807/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-28#a_list)
subject: Data Structures

question: Consider the control flow graph shown in the figure. ![Image](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODdhAQABAPAAAMPDwwAAACwAAAAAAQABAAACAkQBADs=) ![Image](https://practicepaper.in/wp-content/uploads/GATE/CS/20261/q32.webp) Which one of the following options correctly lists the set of redundant expressions (common subexpressions) in the basic blocks B[latex]4[/latex] and B[latex]5[/latex]? Note: All the variables are integers.
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: This question is based on an accompanying control-flow-graph figure showing the statements inside basic blocks B4 and B5. A redundant expression / common subexpression is one that is computed more than once with the same operand values still holding (no intervening redefinition of any operand) at the second computation point, so the second computation could be eliminated and the previously-computed value reused. Working through the statements of B4, only the expression [latex]g*k[/latex] is recomputed later in the block with [latex]g[/latex] and [latex]k[/latex] unchanged in between — so it is the sole common subexpression there. The other candidate ([latex]b+i[/latex]) is not actually redundant once you check that one of its operands gets reassigned before the repeated use, breaking the CSE opportunity. In B5, tracing through similarly shows that the candidate [latex]c+m[/latex] is not a valid common subexpression, because one of its operands ([latex]c[/latex] or [latex]m[/latex]) is redefined between the two apparent uses — so B5 has no redundant expressions at all. Answer: B4 = {g*k}, B5 = { } (empty). Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523048/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-32#a_list)
subject: Compiler Design

question: Consider the following statements about the use of backpatching in a compiler for intermediate code generation: (I) Backpatching can be used to generate code for Boolean expression in one pass. (II) Backpatching can be used to generate code for flow-of-control statements in one pass. Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: (I) Backpatching for Boolean expressions in one pass: TRUE — this is exactly backpatching's classic use case: jump targets for [latex]\text{true}[/latex]/[latex]\text{false}[/latex] lists are left unfilled initially and "patched in" once the actual target address becomes known later, avoiding the need for a second pass. (II) Backpatching for flow-of-control statements (if/while) in one pass: also TRUE — the same technique is used to generate code for conditional and looping constructs single-pass, patching jump instructions once the relevant labels are determined. Answer: Both (I) and (II) are correct. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460824/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-11#a_list)

question: Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?
explanation: [Question 4 Explanation: Live variable analysis determines, at each point in the program, which variables' current values might still be used later (i.e. are "live"). This information is exactly what's needed to decide which variables are worth keeping in fast registers versus which can be safely evicted — that's the core of register allocation/assignment . Run-time function call management, strength reduction, and constant folding are all real optimizations, but none of them fundamentally depend on liveness information the way register allocation does. question: Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU. [latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism. [latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt. Which one of the following options is correct with respect to [latex]\text{S1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{S2}?[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: S1: In a non-vectored interrupt scheme, the CPU typically must poll each device (or run a fixed interrupt-service routine that then figures out which device raised the interrupt) to determine the interrupt source and its ISR address, which takes extra time compared to a vectored scheme where the interrupting device directly supplies (or a lookup table directly provides) the address of its specific ISR. So non-vectored interrupt handling does usually take more time to start the ISR. S1 is true. S2: In a daisy-chain arrangement, devices are connected in series/priority order, and the interrupt-acknowledge signal (or the responsibility of asserting "who interrupted") propagates along the chain itself from device to device — it is not the CPU individually polling every device one by one (that description matches a different scheme, "software polling," not daisy-chaining). So S2 is false. Answer: S1 is true and S2 is false. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523138/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-8#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives: (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction. Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: On an asynchronous interrupt, the processor must first reach a clean state before it can safely switch control: 1. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction — interrupts are only serviced at instruction boundaries, never mid-instruction. 2. (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter — so execution can later resume exactly where it left off. 3. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR — only now does control actually transfer to the ISR. Answer: (iii), (i), (ii) Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460080/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-1#a_list)

[latex] \begin{array}{c} a x+y=b \\ 16 x+a y=24 \end{array} [/latex] Suppose the values of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are chosen such that the system of linear equations produce multiple solutions. Then the product of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: The system [latex]ax+y=b,\ 16x+ay=24[/latex] has infinitely many (multiple) solutions exactly when the two equations describe the same line , i.e. all three coefficient ratios are equal: [latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex] From [latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}[/latex]: [latex]a^2=16\Rightarrow a=\pm4[/latex]. From [latex]\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex]: [latex]b=\dfrac{24}{a}[/latex]. If [latex]a=4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/4=6[/latex], so [latex]ab=4\times6=24[/latex]. If [latex]a=-4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/(-4)=-6[/latex], so [latex]ab=(-4)\times(-6)=24[/latex]. Either valid choice of [latex]a[/latex] gives the same product. Answer: 24 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523125/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-21#a_list)

question: Let [latex]n>1[/latex]. Consider an [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrix [latex]M[/latex] with its elements from [latex]\mathbb{R}[/latex]. Let the vector [latex](0,1,0,0, \ldots, 0) \in \mathbb{R}^{n}[/latex] be in the null space of [latex]M[/latex]. Which of the following options is/are always correct?
options: There are at least two non-zero vectors in the null space of [latex]M[/latex]
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: Since [latex](0,1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex] is in the null space of [latex]M[/latex], we have [latex]M\cdot(0,1,0,\ldots,0)^T=\mathbf{0}[/latex]. But [latex]M[/latex] times this unit vector simply extracts the 2nd column of [latex]M[/latex] . So the 2nd column of [latex]M[/latex] is entirely zero. - Determinant: A matrix with an all-zero column always has determinant [latex]0[/latex]. So "[latex]\det(M)=0[/latex]" is always true. ("[latex]\det(M)=1[/latex]" is always false.) - Rank: The rank could be anywhere from [latex]0[/latex] to [latex]n-1[/latex] depending on the other columns, so "rank [latex]=1[/latex]" is not always true. - Null space size: Since the null space contains the nonzero vector [latex](0,1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], it also contains every scalar multiple of it (e.g. [latex](0,2,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], [latex](0,-1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], etc.), giving infinitely many, hence at least two, distinct non-zero vectors in the null space. This is always true. Answer: Determinant of M is 0; and there are at least two non-zero vectors in the null space of M. question: Consider [latex]4 \times 4[/latex] matrices with their elements from [latex]\{\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}\}[/latex]. The number of such matrices with even number of [latex]\mathbf{1}[/latex] s in every row and every column is
explanation: [Question 5 Explanation: We need [latex]4\times4[/latex] binary matrices where every row and every column has an even number of [latex]1[/latex]s. Freely choose the top-left [latex]3\times3[/latex] sub-block: this can be filled in any of [latex]2^{9}=512[/latex] ways. Once this [latex]3\times3[/latex] block is fixed, the entries in the [latex]4[/latex]th column (for the first [latex]3[/latex] rows) are forced so that each of those rows has an even number of [latex]1[/latex]s, and similarly the entries in the [latex]4[/latex]th row (for the first [latex]3[/latex] columns) are forced by the column parity condition. The single remaining corner entry (row [latex]4[/latex], column [latex]4[/latex]) is then also forced, and it is easy to check the row-[latex]4[/latex] parity and column-[latex]4[/latex] parity conditions become consistent automatically. So the count of valid matrices [latex]=2^{(4-1)^2}=2^9=512[/latex]. Answer: 512 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523078/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-2#a_list)

question: Consider a system of linear equations [latex]P X = Q [/latex] where [latex]P \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} [/latex] and [latex]Q \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1} [/latex]. Suppose [latex]P [/latex] has an [latex]LU [/latex] decomposition, [latex]P = LU [/latex], where [latex] L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ l_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ l_{31} & l_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad U = \begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12} & u_{13} \\ 0 & u_{22} & u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & u_{33} \end{bmatrix} [/latex] Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
options: The system [latex]P X = Q [/latex] can be solved by first solving [latex]L Y = Q [/latex] and then [latex]U X = Y [/latex].
If [latex]P [/latex] is invertible, then both [latex]L [/latex] and [latex]U [/latex] are invertible.
If [latex]P [/latex] is singular, then at least one of the diagonal elements of [latex]U [/latex] is zero.
If [latex]P [/latex] is symmetric, then both [latex]L [/latex] and [latex]U [/latex] are symmetric.
explanation: [Question 6 Explanation: Solving via [latex]LY=Q[/latex] then [latex]UX=Y[/latex]: substituting [latex]P=LU[/latex] into [latex]PX=Q[/latex] gives [latex]L(UX)=Q[/latex]; setting [latex]Y=UX[/latex], we solve [latex]LY=Q[/latex] first (easy, forward substitution since [latex]L[/latex] is lower triangular), then [latex]UX=Y[/latex] (easy, back substitution). True — this is exactly the standard LU-solve method. If [latex]P[/latex] is invertible, both [latex]L,U[/latex] invertible: [latex]L[/latex] is unit lower-triangular (diagonal all [latex]1[/latex]s), so [latex]\det(L)=1[/latex] always, regardless of [latex]P[/latex] — [latex]L[/latex] is always invertible. Since [latex]\det(P)=\det(L)\det(U)=\det(U)[/latex], if [latex]P[/latex] is invertible ([latex]\det(P)\ne0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)\ne0[/latex] too. True. If [latex]P[/latex] singular, some diagonal element of [latex]U[/latex] is zero: since [latex]\det(P)=\det(U)[/latex] (product of [latex]U[/latex]'s diagonal, as [latex]U[/latex] is upper triangular), if [latex]P[/latex] is singular ([latex]\det(P)=0[/latex]) then [latex]\det(U)=0[/latex], which for a triangular matrix forces at least one diagonal entry to be [latex]0[/latex]. True. If [latex]P[/latex] symmetric, both [latex]L,U[/latex] symmetric: plain LU decomposition does not generally preserve/reveal symmetry in [latex]L[/latex] and [latex]U[/latex] individually (that requires a specialized decomposition like [latex]LDL^T[/latex] or Cholesky). False in general. Answer: The first three statements are TRUE; the last (about symmetric P forcing symmetric L,U) is FALSE. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460801/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-34#a_list)

question: Let [latex]L [/latex], [latex]M [/latex], and [latex]N [/latex] be non-singular matrices of order 3 satisfying the equations [latex] L^2 = L^{-1}, \quad M = L^8, \quad N = L^2. [/latex] Which ONE of the following is the value of the determinant of [latex](M - N) [/latex]?
explanation: [Question 7 Explanation: From [latex]L^2=L^{-1}[/latex], multiply both sides by [latex]L[/latex]: [latex]L^3=L^2\cdot L=L^{-1}\cdot L=I[/latex]. So [latex]L[/latex] has order dividing [latex]3[/latex]. [latex]M=L^8=L^{6+2}=(L^3)^2\cdot L^2=I^2\cdot L^2=L^2[/latex]. But we're also given [latex]N=L^2[/latex]. So [latex]M=N[/latex] exactly, meaning [latex]M-N[/latex] is the zero matrix. [latex]\det(M-N)=\det(0)=0[/latex] Answer: 0 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460831/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-4#a_list)

question: [latex] A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, [/latex] then which ONE of the following is [latex]A^8 [/latex]?
explanation: [Question 8 Explanation: Eigenvalues of [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex]: [latex](1-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)-4=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2-1-4=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2=5\Rightarrow\lambda=\pm\sqrt5[/latex] Since [latex]A[/latex] is symmetric, it's diagonalizable with these eigenvalues, and [latex]A^8[/latex] has eigenvalues [latex](\sqrt5)^8=5^4=625[/latex] and [latex](-\sqrt5)^8=625[/latex] as well (both eigenvalues raised to an even power give the same positive result). Since both eigenvalues of [latex]A^8[/latex] equal [latex]625[/latex], [latex]A^8[/latex] is simply the scalar matrix [latex]625I[/latex]. Answer: [[625,0],[0,625]] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460834/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-1#a_list)
subject: Engineering Mathematics

question: Let [latex]A[/latex] be a 2x2 matrix as given: [latex]A = \left[\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right][/latex] What are the eigenvalues of the matrix [latex]A^{13}[/latex]?
explanation: [Question 9 Explanation: Find the eigenvalues of [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex] from its characteristic equation: [latex](1-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)-1\times1=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^2-1-1=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^2=2\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=\pm\sqrt2[/latex] If [latex]\lambda[/latex] is an eigenvalue of [latex]A[/latex], then [latex]\lambda^{13}[/latex] is the corresponding eigenvalue of [latex]A^{13}[/latex] (eigenvalues of a matrix power are just the original eigenvalues raised to that power): [latex](\sqrt2)^{13}=2^{13/2}=2^{6}\cdot2^{1/2}=64\sqrt2[/latex], and similarly [latex](-\sqrt2)^{13}=-64\sqrt2[/latex]. Answer: 64√2, -64√2 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460049/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-31#a_list)

explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: We want a recursive count of nodes in a non-empty singly linked list. The natural recursive base case is: if the current node is the last node (i.e. [latex]\text{head->next==NULL}[/latex]), then this contributes exactly [latex]1[/latex] to the count, so [latex]\text{E1: head->next==NULL}[/latex], returning [latex]1[/latex]. Otherwise, the count is [latex]1[/latex] (for the current node) plus however many nodes remain in the rest of the list starting from [latex]\text{head->next}[/latex]: [latex]\text{E2: 1+getListSize(head->next)}[/latex]. (Using [latex]\text{head==NULL}[/latex] as the base case instead would also work logically for a possibly-empty list, but here the function is documented to be called only on a non-empty list, and combined with the given E2 form, the option that consistently checks [latex]\text{head->next}[/latex] in the base case and recurses on [latex]\text{head->next}[/latex] is the matching, correct pair.) question: Consider a processor that has [latex]16[/latex] general purpose registers and it uses [latex]2[/latex]-byte instruction format for all its instructions. Variable-sized opcodes are permitted. There are three different types of instructions; M-type, R-type, and C-type. Each M-type instruction has [latex]2[/latex] register operands and a [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate operand. Each Rtype instruction has [latex]3[/latex] register operands. Each C-type instruction has a register operand and a [latex]6[/latex] -bit offset value. If there are [latex]2[/latex] unique M-type opcodes and [latex]7[/latex] unique R-type opcodes, which one of the following options gives the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: With [latex]16[/latex] general-purpose registers, each register operand needs [latex]\log_2 16=4[/latex] bits. The full instruction is [latex]2[/latex] bytes [latex]=16[/latex] bits. - M-type: [latex]2[/latex] register operands ([latex]8[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate [latex]=14[/latex] bits of operand, leaving [latex]16-14=2[/latex] bits for the opcode → up to [latex]2^2=4[/latex] possible M-type codes, but only [latex]2[/latex] are actually used, leaving [latex]4-2=2[/latex] unused [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes free for other instruction types. - R-type: [latex]3[/latex] register operands ([latex]12[/latex] bits), leaving [latex]16-12=4[/latex] bits for the opcode. Using an "expanding opcode" scheme, the [latex]2[/latex] leftover [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes (not used by M-type) each expand into [latex]2^{4-2}=4[/latex] possible [latex]4[/latex]-bit codes, giving [latex]2\times4=8[/latex] total available R-type slots; only [latex]7[/latex] are used, leaving [latex]8-7=1[/latex] unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix. - C-type: [latex]1[/latex] register operand ([latex]4[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit offset [latex]=10[/latex] bits, leaving [latex]16-10=6[/latex] bits for the opcode. That single unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix expands into [latex]2^{6-4}=4[/latex] possible [latex]6[/latex]-bit C-type codes. Answer: 4 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523112/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-34#a_list)

question: Consider a processor [latex]\text{P}[/latex] whose instruction set architecture is the load-store architecture. The instruction format is such that the first operand of any instruction is the destination operand. Which one of the following sequences of instructions corresponds to the high-level language statement [latex]{Z}={X}+{Y}[/latex] ? Note: X, Y, and Z are memory operands. R[latex]0[/latex], R[latex]1[/latex], and R[latex]2[/latex] are registers.
options: LOAD R[latex]0[/latex], X ADD Z, R[latex]0[/latex], Y
ADD R[latex]0[/latex], X, Y STORE Z, R[latex]0[/latex]
LOAD R[latex]0[/latex], X LOAD R[latex]1[/latex], Y ADD R[latex]2[/latex], R[latex]0[/latex], R[latex]1[/latex] STORE Z, R[latex]2[/latex]
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: In a load-store (register-register) architecture, arithmetic instructions can only operate on registers, never directly on memory. So to compute [latex]Z=X+Y[/latex] where [latex]X,Y,Z[/latex] are memory locations, we must: 1. LOAD both memory operands into registers: [latex]\text{LOAD } R0, X[/latex] and [latex]\text{LOAD } R1, Y[/latex]. 2. Perform the addition on registers: [latex]\text{ADD } R2, R0, R1[/latex] (destination is first operand, per the given convention). 3. STORE the result back to memory: [latex]\text{STORE } Z, R2[/latex]. Any option that uses a memory operand directly inside an ADD instruction (e.g. [latex]\text{ADD } Z, X, Y[/latex] or [latex]\text{ADD } Z, R0, Y[/latex]) is invalid for a load-store machine, since ADD can only take register operands. Answer: LOAD R0,X; LOAD R1,Y; ADD R2,R0,R1; STORE Z,R2 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523075/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-5#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: An application executes [latex]6.4 \times 10^8[/latex] number of instructions in 6.3 seconds. There are four types of instructions, the details of which are given in the table. The duration of a clock cycle in nanoseconds is _________. (rounded off to one decimal place)[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Instruction type} & \text{Clock cycles required per instruction (CPI)} & \text{Number of instructions executed} \\ \hline \text{Branch} & 2 & 2.25 \times 10^8 \\ \text{Load} & 5 & 1.20 \times 10^8 \\ \text{Store} & 4 & 1.65 \times 10^8 \\ \text{Arithmetic} & 3 & 1.30 \times 10^8 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: Total clock cycles [latex]=\sum(\text{CPI}\times\text{count})[/latex]: [latex]=2(2.25\times10^8)+5(1.20\times10^8)+4(1.65\times10^8)+3(1.30\times10^8)[/latex] [latex]=4.5\times10^8+6.0\times10^8+6.6\times10^8+3.9\times10^8=21.0\times10^8=2.1\times10^9[/latex] cycles. Clock cycle duration [latex]=\dfrac{\text{total time}}{\text{total cycles}}=\dfrac{6.3\text{ s}}{2.1\times10^9}=3\times10^{-9}\text{ s}=3[/latex] ns. Answer: 3 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460842/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-51#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: Which of the following is/are part of an Instruction Set Architecture of a processor?
options: The size of the cache memory
The clock frequency of the processor
The number of cache memory levels
explanation: [Question 4 Explanation: The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the software-visible contract between hardware and software — things like available instructions, addressing modes, and the visible register set. The total number of (architecturally visible) registers is part of this contract, since programs/compilers must know how many registers they can target. Cache size, clock frequency, and number of cache levels are all microarchitecture (implementation) details — two processors implementing the very same ISA can freely differ in these without breaking software compatibility. Answer: The total number of registers Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460817/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-18#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: A processor has 64 general-purpose registers and 50 distinct instruction types. An instruction is encoded in 32-bits. What is the maximum number of bits that can be used to store the immediate operand for the given instruction? ADD R1, #25 // R1 = R1 + 25
explanation: [Question 5 Explanation: With [latex]64=2^6[/latex] registers, each register-number field needs [latex]6[/latex] bits. With [latex]50[/latex] distinct instruction types, the opcode field needs [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] bits (since [latex]2^5=32<50\le64=2^6[/latex]). The instruction [latex]\text{ADD R1, \#25}[/latex] (meaning [latex]\text{R1}=\text{R1}+25[/latex]) only needs to name one register (used as both source and destination), plus an immediate value. So the [latex]32[/latex]-bit instruction splits as: opcode ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] one register field ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] immediate field (the rest). Immediate field width [latex]=32-6-6=20[/latex] bits. Answer: 20 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460053/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-27#a_list)

question: Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are [latex]8[/latex] holes in the memory of sizes [latex]20 \text{KB}, 4 \text{KB}[/latex], [latex]25 \text{KB}, 18 \text{KB}, 7 \text{KB}, 9 \text{KB}, 15 \text{KB}[/latex], and [latex]12\text{KB}[/latex]. Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] of size [latex]16KB[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex] of size [latex]9KB[/latex] arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex], the number of holes of size less than [latex]8KB[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer) Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Best-fit always picks the smallest hole that is still large enough to satisfy the request. Initial holes (KB): [latex]20,4,25,18,7,9,15,12[/latex]. P1 (16 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge16[/latex] is [latex]18[/latex]. Allocate there, leaving a remainder hole of [latex]18-16=2[/latex] KB. Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,9,15,12,2[/latex]. P2 (9 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge9[/latex] is the exact-fit [latex]9[/latex] KB hole itself, which is fully consumed (disappears entirely). Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,15,12,2[/latex] ([latex]7[/latex] holes remaining). Counting holes smaller than [latex]8[/latex] KB among [latex]\{20,4,25,7,15,12,2\}[/latex]: [latex]4[/latex] KB, [latex]7[/latex] KB, and [latex]2[/latex] KB — exactly [latex]3[/latex] holes. question: A system has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) that has a reach of [latex]1[/latex] MB. TLB reach is defined as the total amount of physical memory that can be accessed through the TLB entries. The paging system uses pages of size [latex]4[/latex] KB. The virtual address space is [latex]64[/latex] GB and physical address space is [latex]1[/latex] GB. If each TLB entry stores a [latex]4[/latex]-bit process id, page number, frame number, and a [latex]2[/latex]-bit control field, then the size of the TLB (in bytes) is ________. (answer in integer) Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}, 1 {M}=2^{20}, 1 {G}=2^{30}[/latex]
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: TLB reach [latex]=[/latex] page size [latex]\times[/latex] number of TLB entries, so number of entries [latex]=\dfrac{1\text{ MB}}{4\text{ KB}}=\dfrac{2^{20}}{2^{12}}=2^8=256[/latex] entries. Virtual address space [latex]=64\text{ GB}=2^{36}[/latex] bytes, so virtual page number [latex]=36-12=24[/latex] bits (page size [latex]4\text{ KB}=2^{12}[/latex]). Physical address space [latex]=1\text{ GB}=2^{30}[/latex] bytes, so frame number [latex]=30-12=18[/latex] bits. Each TLB entry stores: [latex]4[/latex]-bit PID [latex]+[/latex] [latex]24[/latex]-bit page number [latex]+[/latex] [latex]18[/latex]-bit frame number [latex]+[/latex] [latex]2[/latex]-bit control [latex]=4+24+18+2=48[/latex] bits [latex]=6[/latex] bytes per entry. Total TLB size [latex]=256\times6=1536[/latex] bytes. Answer: 1536 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523102/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-44#a_list)
subject: Operating System

question: Consider a system that has a cache memory unit and a memory management unit (MMU). The address input to the cache memory is a physical address. The MMU has a translation lookaside buffer (TLB). Assume that when a page is evicted from the main memory, the corresponding blocks in the cache are marked as invalid. For a given memory reference, which of the following sequences of events can NEVER happen?
options: TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit
TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit
TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit
TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: A memory reference passes through, in order: TLB → (page table, only if TLB misses) → cache. - TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit: possible — TLB doesn't have the mapping, page table does (page is in memory), and the corresponding cache block (whose validity depends on the page being resident) can indeed be valid and hit. Can happen. - TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible . A TLB hit means the page is currently mapped/resident in memory (TLB entries are only valid for pages currently in memory); it is therefore contradictory for the page table to then report a miss (page not in memory) for that very same page. - TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible . A page-table miss means the page is not in main memory at all — and the problem states that when a page is evicted, its cache blocks are marked invalid. So if the page isn't in memory, its cache blocks cannot be valid, and a cache hit is impossible. - TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss: possible and in fact the expected/consistent sequence when a page is genuinely not resident. Answer: "TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit" and "TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit" can NEVER happen. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523036/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-44#a_list)
subject: Operating System

question: Consider a complete graph [latex]K_{n}[/latex] with [latex]n[/latex] vertices ( [latex]n>4[/latex] ). Note that multiple spanning trees can be constructed over [latex]K_{n}[/latex]. Each of these spanning trees is represented as a set of edges. The Jaccard coefficient between any two sets is defined as the ratio of the size of the intersection of the two sets to the size of the union of the two sets. Which one of the following options gives the lowest possible value for the Jaccard coefficient between any two spanning trees of [latex]K_{n}[/latex] ?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: The Jaccard coefficient between two spanning-tree edge sets is [latex]\dfrac{|E_1\cap E_2|}{|E_1\cup E_2|}[/latex], which reaches its lowest possible value [latex]0[/latex] precisely when the two spanning trees share no edges at all (completely edge-disjoint spanning trees). In [latex]K_n[/latex] for [latex]n>4[/latex], there are more than enough edges ([latex]\binom{n}{2}[/latex] total, versus only [latex]n-1[/latex] needed per spanning tree) to always construct two entirely edge-disjoint spanning trees (this is guaranteed by well-known results on edge-disjoint spanning trees in dense graphs, e.g. via Nash-Williams/Tutte-style constructions). When the intersection is empty, the Jaccard coefficient is exactly [latex]0[/latex], which is also the theoretical minimum possible value for any Jaccard coefficient. Answer: 0 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523120/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-26#a_list)
subject: Algorithms

question: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a simple, undirected, edge-weighted graph with unique edge weights. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees (MST) of [latex]G[/latex] is/are true?
options: In every cycle [latex]C[/latex] of [latex]G[/latex], the edge with the largest weight in [latex]C[/latex] is not in any MST
In every cycle [latex]C[/latex] of [latex]G[/latex], the edge with the smallest weight in [latex]C[/latex] is in every MST
For every vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], the edge with the largest weight incident on [latex]v[/latex] is not in any MST
For every vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], the edge with the smallest weight incident on [latex]v[/latex] is in every MST
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: When all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique , and two classical facts (cycle property and cut property) apply: - Cycle property: In any cycle [latex]C[/latex], the edge with the strictly largest weight can never appear in any MST (if it did, removing it and adding any other edge of the cycle would still keep the graph connected but reduce total weight). True. - The claim about the smallest -weight edge of every cycle being in every MST is false in general — a small edge can still be excluded if a smaller alternative path already connects its endpoints via other, even-cheaper edges from elsewhere in the graph (cycle property only rules out the *maximum*, it doesn't force in the minimum in the multi-cycle case with unrelated cycles overlapping). - The claim that the largest -weight edge touching any given vertex [latex]v[/latex] is never in any MST is false — that edge might still be the cheapest way to connect an isolated/far-off part of the graph. - Cut property: For any vertex [latex]v[/latex], consider the cut separating [latex]\{v\}[/latex] from the rest of the graph; the minimum-weight edge crossing this cut (i.e. the cheapest edge incident to [latex]v[/latex]) must belong to every MST, since choosing any costlier edge to connect [latex]v[/latex] instead would strictly increase total weight. True. Answer: The largest-weight edge in every cycle is excluded from every MST; and the smallest-weight edge incident to every vertex is included in every MST. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523041/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-39#a_list)
subject: Algorithms

Host bits [latex]=32-20=12[/latex], giving [latex]2^{12}=4096[/latex] total addresses in the subnet. Of these, [latex]2[/latex] are reserved (the all-zeros network address and the all-ones broadcast address) and cannot be assigned to interfaces. Usable addresses [latex]=4096-2=4094[/latex]. question: An ISP having an address block [latex]202.16.0.0/15[/latex] assigns a block of [latex]6000[/latex] IP addresses to a client, using the classless internet domain routing (CIDR) super-netting approach. Which of the following address blocks can be assigned by the ISP?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: The ISP's block [latex]202.16.0.0/15[/latex] spans two full class-B-sized blocks: all addresses from [latex]202.16.0.0[/latex] to [latex]202.17.255.255[/latex]. For [latex]6000[/latex] addresses via CIDR super-netting, we need a block with at least [latex]6000[/latex] addresses; a [latex]/19[/latex] prefix gives [latex]2^{32-19}=2^{13}=8192[/latex] addresses, which suffices (a [latex]/20[/latex] would only give [latex]4096<6000[/latex]). A valid [latex]/19[/latex] sub-block must (a) lie entirely within [latex]202.16.0.0[/latex]-[latex]202.17.255.255[/latex], and (b) have its network address aligned to a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] in the relevant octet (since [latex]/19[/latex] leaves [latex]13[/latex] host bits, and [latex]2^{13}=8192=32\times256[/latex] addresses per block, so the 3rd octet must be a multiple of [latex]32[/latex]: [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]). - [latex]202.16.0.0/19[/latex]: [latex]0[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], and within range. Valid. - [latex]202.17.64.0/19[/latex]: [latex]64[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], [latex]202.17.x[/latex] is within the /15 range. Valid. - [latex]202.16.32.0/19[/latex]: [latex]32[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex]. Valid. - [latex]202.17.24.0/19[/latex]: [latex]24[/latex] is not a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] (valid boundaries are [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]), so this is not a properly aligned [latex]/19[/latex] block. Invalid. Answer: 202.16.0.0/19, 202.17.64.0/19, and 202.16.32.0/19 can be assigned. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523034/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-46#a_list)

question: In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set [latex]\text{F}[/latex] of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by [latex]\text{F}[/latex] is called the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex]. To compute the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex], Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider [latex]X, Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows. Reflexivity: If [latex]Y \subseteq X[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] Augmentation: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex], then [latex]X Z \rightarrow Y Z[/latex] for any Z Transitivity: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]Y \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex] The additional rule of Union is defined as follows. Union: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y Z[/latex] It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: The standard proof of the Union rule ([latex]X\to Y,\,X\to Z\;\Rightarrow\;X\to YZ[/latex]) proceeds as follows: 1. [latex]X\to Y[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]X[/latex] to both sides): [latex]X\to XY[/latex] (using [latex]XX=X[/latex]). 2. [latex]X\to Z[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]Y[/latex] to both sides): [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex]. 3. Combining steps 1 and 2 via Transitivity : [latex]X\to XY[/latex] and [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex] gives [latex]X\to YZ[/latex]. This derivation only ever invokes Augmentation and Transitivity — Reflexivity is never needed anywhere in the chain. So these two rules alone are both necessary (the proof genuinely needs both types of steps) and sufficient (nothing else is required). Answer: Augmentation and Transitivity Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523114/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-32#a_list)
subject: Database Management System

question: In the context of relational database normalization, which of the following statements is/are true?
options: It is always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving [latex]3[/latex]NF decomposition of a relation
It is always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving [latex]1[/latex]NF decomposition of a relation
It is not always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition of a relation
It is not always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving [latex]2[/latex]NF decomposition of a relation
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Standard relational-normalization theory results: - 3NF: It is a classical theorem that every relation schema has a dependency-preserving (and lossless-join) decomposition into 3NF, via the synthesis algorithm on a minimal cover of the FDs. True. - 1NF: 1NF only requires atomic domains; a relation can always trivially satisfy/preserve 1NF without needing to give up any functional dependency (no decomposition is even forced). True. - BCNF: It is a well-known counterexample-backed result that a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition is not always possible — achieving BCNF can force us to lose some functional dependency (they can only be checked by joining relations back together, which is expensive/impossible to enforce locally). True (i.e., "not always possible" is a true statement). - 2NF: Since a dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition always exists, and 3NF automatically implies 2NF, a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition is always achievable too. So "it is not always possible to get a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition" is false . Answer: Dependency-preserving decompositions always exist for 3NF and for 1NF; it is not always possible for BCNF. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523059/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-21#a_list)

explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Decode [latex]0\text{xC2710000}[/latex] as IEEE-754 single precision: Binary: sign bit [latex]=1[/latex] (negative); exponent bits [latex]=10000100_2=132[/latex], unbiased exponent [latex]=132-127=5[/latex]; mantissa bits [latex]=11100010000000000000000[/latex]. Mantissa value [latex]=1+2^{-1}+2^{-2}+2^{-3}+2^{-7}=1+0.5+0.25+0.125+0.0078125=1.8828125[/latex]. Value [latex]=-1.8828125\times2^{5}=-1.8828125\times32=-60.25[/latex]. Answer: -60.25 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523122/gate-cse-2024-set-2-question-24#a_list)
subject: Digital Logic

question: In a system, numbers are represented using [latex]4[/latex]-bit two's complement form. Consider four numbers [latex]N 1=1011, N 2=1101, N 3=1010[/latex] and [latex]N 4=1001[/latex] in the system. Which of the following operations will result in arithmetic overflow?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Convert each 4-bit two's-complement number to its signed decimal value (invert bits and add [latex]1[/latex] if the leading bit is [latex]1[/latex]): [latex]N1{=}1011\to-5,\ N2{=}1101\to-3,\ N3{=}1010\to-6,\ N4{=}1001\to-7[/latex]. The representable range for [latex]4[/latex]-bit two's complement is [latex][-8,7][/latex]; a result falling outside this range signals overflow. - [latex]N1+N2=-5+(-3)=-8[/latex] → within range. No overflow. - [latex]N2+N3=-3+(-6)=-9[/latex] → below [latex]-8[/latex]. Overflow. - [latex]N3-N4=-6-(-7)=1[/latex] → within range. No overflow. - [latex]N1+N4=-5+(-7)=-12[/latex] → below [latex]-8[/latex]. Overflow. Answer: N2+N3 and N1+N4 cause arithmetic overflow. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523128/gate-cse-1826-set-2-question-18#a_list)
subject: Digital Logic

question: Consider the real valued variables [latex]X, Y[/latex] and [latex]Z[/latex] represented using the IEEE [latex]754[/latex] singleprecision floating-point format. The binary representations of [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] in hexadecimal notation are as follows: [latex] X: 35 {C} 00000 \quad Y: 34 {A} 00000 [/latex] Let [latex]Z=X+Y[/latex]. Which one of the following is the binary representation of [latex]Z[/latex], in hexadecimal notation?
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: Decode both IEEE-754 single-precision numbers (format: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits [bias 127], 23 mantissa bits): [latex]X=35\text{C}00000_{16}[/latex] → sign [latex]=0[/latex], exponent bits [latex]=01101011_2=107[/latex] (unbiased [latex]=107-127=-20[/latex]), mantissa [latex]=1.1_2[/latex]. So [latex]X=1.1_2\times2^{-20}[/latex]. [latex]Y=34\text{A}00000_{16}[/latex] → sign [latex]=0[/latex], exponent bits [latex]=01101001_2=105[/latex] (unbiased [latex]=-22[/latex]), mantissa [latex]=1.01_2[/latex]. So [latex]Y=1.01_2\times2^{-22}[/latex]. To add, align [latex]Y[/latex]'s exponent to [latex]-20[/latex] by shifting its mantissa right by [latex]2[/latex] bits: [latex]Y=0.0101_2\times2^{-20}[/latex]. [latex]X+Y=(1.1000_2+0.0101_2)\times2^{-20}=1.1101_2\times2^{-20}[/latex]. This is already normalized (leading digit [latex]1[/latex], no need to shift the exponent). So [latex]Z[/latex] has the same exponent as [latex]X[/latex] (exponent bits [latex]01101011[/latex]) and mantissa [latex]1101\underbrace{0\ldots0}_{19\text{ zeros}}[/latex], giving hex [latex]35\text{E}80000[/latex]. Answer: 35E80000 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523054/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-26#a_list)
subject: Digital Logic

question: Consider the [latex]8[/latex] -bit signed integers [latex]X, Y[/latex] and [latex]Z[/latex] represented using the sign-magnitude form. The binary representations of [latex]X[/latex] and [latex]Y[/latex] are as follows: [latex] X: 10110100 \quad Y: 01001100 [/latex] Which of the following operations to compute [latex]Z[/latex] result(s) in an arithmetic overflow?
explanation: [Question 4 Explanation: In 8-bit sign-magnitude form, bit 7 is the sign and bits 6-0 give the magnitude (max magnitude [latex]=127[/latex]). [latex]X=10110100[/latex]: sign [latex]=1[/latex] (negative), magnitude [latex]=0110100_2=52[/latex], so [latex]X=-52[/latex]. [latex]Y=01001100[/latex]: sign [latex]=0[/latex] (positive), magnitude [latex]=1001100_2=76[/latex], so [latex]Y=+76[/latex]. Overflow happens whenever the true arithmetic result's magnitude exceeds [latex]127[/latex] (i.e. falls outside [latex][-127,127][/latex]): - [latex]X+Y=-52+76=24[/latex] → within range, no overflow . - [latex]X-Y=-52-76=-128[/latex] → magnitude [latex]128>127[/latex], overflow . - [latex]-X+Y=52+76=128[/latex] → magnitude [latex]128>127[/latex], overflow . - [latex]-X-Y=52-76=-24[/latex] → within range, no overflow . Answer: Z = X - Y, and Z = -X + Y Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523068/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-12#a_list)
subject: Digital Logic

question: Three floating point numbers [latex]X, Y, Z [/latex] are stored in three registers [latex]RX, RY, RZ [/latex], respectively in IEEE 754 single precision format as given below in hexadecimal: [latex] RX = 0\times C1100000, \quad RY = 0\times 40C00000, \quad RZ = 0 \times 41400000 [/latex] Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
explanation: [Question 5 Explanation: Decoding the IEEE-754 single-precision hex values: [latex]RX=0\text{xC1100000}\to X=-9[/latex], [latex]RY=0\text{x40C00000}\to Y=6[/latex], [latex]RZ=0\text{x41400000}\to Z=12[/latex]. Checking each option: - [latex]4(X+Y)+Z=4(-9+6)+12=4(-3)+12=-12+12=0[/latex]. True. - [latex]2Y-Z=2(6)-12=12-12=0[/latex]. True. - [latex]4X+3Z=4(-9)+3(12)=-36+36=0[/latex]. True. - [latex]X+Y+Z=-9+6+12=9\ne0[/latex]. False. Answer: 4(X+Y)+Z=0; 2Y-Z=0; and 4X+3Z=0 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460796/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-39#a_list)
subject: Digital Logic

question: The following two signed 2's complement numbers (multiplicand [latex]M [/latex] and multiplier [latex]Q [/latex]) are being multiplied using Booth's algorithm: [latex] M: 1100 \, 1101 \, 1110 \, 1101 \quad \text{and} \quad Q: 1010 \, 0100 \, 1010 \, 1010 [/latex] The total number of addition and subtraction operations to be performed is ________. (Answer in integer)
explanation: [Question 6 Explanation: In Booth's algorithm, an addition or subtraction is performed at every bit-position where the pair (current [latex]Q_0[/latex] bit, previous bit [latex]Q_{-1}[/latex], initialized to [latex]0[/latex]) shows a transition ("01" → add [latex]M[/latex], "10" → subtract [latex]M[/latex]); a run of identical bits ("00" or "11") triggers no arithmetic operation, just a shift. Scanning [latex]Q=1010\,0100\,1010\,1010[/latex] (appended with the initial [latex]Q_{-1}=0[/latex]) for every "01" or "10" transition between consecutive bit pairs gives [latex]13[/latex] such transition points out of the [latex]16[/latex] total bit-positions. Answer: 13 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460813/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-22#a_list)
subject: Digital Logic

question: The number [latex]-6[/latex] can be represented as 1010 in 4-bit 2's complement representation. Which of the following is/are CORRECT 2's complement representation(s) of [latex]-6[/latex]?
explanation: [Question 7 Explanation: Correctly extending a two's-complement number to more bits requires sign-extension : replicate the sign bit (here, the leading [latex]1[/latex], since [latex]-6[/latex] is negative) into all the new higher-order bit positions — you cannot just prepend arbitrary/zero bits. [latex]-6[/latex] in 4-bit: [latex]1010[/latex]. Correct 8-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1010[/latex] (four [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,1010[/latex] incorrectly prepends [latex]1000[/latex] instead of replicating the sign bit — wrong. Correct 16-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1111\,1111\,1010[/latex] (twelve [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,0000\,0000\,1010[/latex] is similarly wrong. Answer: 1111 1010 (8-bit) and 1111 1111 1111 1010 (16-bit) Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460065/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-15#a_list)
subject: Digital Logic

question: A day can only be cloudy or sunny. The probability of a day being cloudy is [latex]0.5[/latex], independent of the condition on other days. What is the probability that in any given four days, there will be three cloudy days and one sunny day?

question: In the [latex]2020[/latex] summer Olympics' Javelin throw finals, Neeraj Chopra exhibited a spectacular performance to win the gold medal. The silver medal was won by Jakub Vadlejch and the bronze medal was won by Vitezlav Vesely. There were six rounds of throws with each athlete having one throw per round. The best of all the throws of each athlete is considered for the medal. Following were the observations about the throws: i.) The first and second rounds were dominated by Neeraj Chopra with a gold medal performance in his second throw, while the other two athletes did not have any medal winning throws in these rounds. ii.) The throws in the last round by both Jakub Vadlejch and Vitezlav Vesely were fouls and were not considered for scoring. iii.) After four rounds, Vitezlav Vesely was in the second position and could not improve upon his best throw in the succeeding rounds. iv.) In the fourth round, the throw by Jakub Vadlejch was the best in that round. In which round did Vitezlav Vesely have his best throw?
explanation: [Question 8 Explanation: Work through the clues step by step: (i) Rounds [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]2[/latex] belong entirely to Neeraj Chopra (his 2nd throw was gold-medal-worthy); Jakub and Vesely achieved none of their medal-relevant (best) throws in these two rounds. So neither Jakub's nor Vesely's personal-best throw happened in round 1 or 2 — both of their best throws must fall somewhere in rounds [latex]3[/latex]-[latex]6[/latex]. (ii) Both Jakub's and Vesely's round-[latex]6[/latex] throws were fouls (not counted at all), so neither of their best throws can be in round [latex]6[/latex] either. This narrows their best throws down to rounds [latex]3,4,5[/latex]. (iii) After [latex]4[/latex] rounds, Vesely already held [latex]2[/latex]nd position, and he never improved on this best throw afterward (rounds [latex]5[/latex] and [latex]6[/latex] didn't help him). So Vesely's personal-best throw must have occurred within rounds [latex]1[/latex]-[latex]4[/latex] — combined with the earlier elimination of rounds [latex]1,2[/latex], this leaves only round [latex]3[/latex] or round [latex]4[/latex] as candidates. (iv) In round [latex]4[/latex], it was Jakub's throw that was the best of that round (not Vesely's) — this is consistent with Vesely's personal best having already been set earlier, in round [latex]3[/latex], and round [latex]4[/latex] simply being a round where Jakub (not Vesely) peaked. Putting it together, Vesely's best throw was in round 3 . Answer: Third Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523081/gate-cse-2026-set-1-ga-question-9#a_list)

question: For positive real numbers [latex]S[/latex] and [latex]K[/latex], the function [latex]H_{K}(S)[/latex] is defined as: [latex]H_{K}(S)=\max (S-K, 0)[/latex]. The max function is defined as: [latex] \max (a, b)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} a, & \text { when } a>b \\ b, & \text { when } a \leq b \end{array}\right. [/latex] The graph below shows the plot of a function [latex]N(S)[/latex] versus [latex]S[/latex]. [latex]N(S)[/latex] can be expressed as ________. ![Image](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODdhAQABAPAAAMPDwwAAACwAAAAAAQABAAACAkQBADs=) ![Image](https://practicepaper.in/wp-content/uploads/GATE/CS/20261/q63.webp)
explanation: [Question 9 Explanation: [latex]H_K(S)=\max(S-K,0)[/latex] is the standard "ramp"/hinge function: it is [latex]0[/latex] for [latex]S\le K[/latex], and rises linearly with slope [latex]1[/latex] for [latex]S>K[/latex]. The plotted function [latex]N(S)[/latex] (from the figure) is [latex]0[/latex] up to [latex]S=10[/latex], then rises with slope [latex]1[/latex] from [latex]S=10[/latex] to [latex]S=20[/latex], and then becomes flat (constant) again for [latex]S>20[/latex] — a shape that increases and then saturates. This exact shape is produced by taking one upward ramp starting at [latex]10[/latex] and cancelling its slope beyond [latex]20[/latex] using a second ramp of opposite sign starting at [latex]20[/latex]: [latex]N(S)=H_{10}(S)-H_{20}(S)[/latex] For [latex]S\le10[/latex]: both terms are [latex]0[/latex] → [latex]N=0[/latex]. For [latex]10 20[/latex]: [latex]H_{10}(S)=S-10[/latex], [latex]H_{20}(S)=S-20[/latex] → [latex]N=(S-10)-(S-20)=10[/latex] (flat/saturated), matching the graph. Answer: [latex]H_{10}(S)-H_{20}(S)[/latex] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523082/gate-cse-2026-set-1-ga-question-8#a_list)

question: In the given figure, PQRS is a square of side 2 cm and PLMN is a rectangle. The corner L of the rectangle is on the side QR. Side MN of the rectangle passes through the corner S of the square. What is the area (in [latex]cm^{2} [/latex]) of the rectangle PLMN? Note: The figure shown is representative. ![Image](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODdhAQABAPAAAMPDwwAAACwAAAAAAQABAAACAkQBADs=) ![Image](https://practicepaper.in/wp-content/uploads/GATE/CS/20252/q64.webp)
explanation: [Question 14 Explanation: Set up coordinates matching the figure: [latex]P=(0,2),\ Q=(0,0),\ R=(2,0),\ S=(2,2)[/latex] (square side [latex]2[/latex]). Let [latex]L=(\ell,0)[/latex] be the point on [latex]QR[/latex] where the rectangle's corner lands. Side [latex]PL[/latex] has direction vector [latex](\ell,-2)[/latex] and length [latex]\sqrt{\ell^2+4}[/latex]. Since [latex]PLMN[/latex] is a rectangle, side [latex]LM[/latex] is perpendicular to [latex]PL[/latex], along direction [latex](2,\ell)/\sqrt{\ell^2+4}[/latex]. If the rectangle's width (side [latex]LM[/latex]) is [latex]h[/latex], then: [latex]N=P+h\cdot\dfrac{(2,\ell)}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}},\qquad M=L+h\cdot\dfrac{(2,\ell)}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}[/latex] Since side [latex]MN[/latex] must pass through [latex]S=(2,2)[/latex], substituting [latex]S[/latex] into the line through [latex]M,N[/latex] (which runs parallel to [latex]PL[/latex], direction [latex](\ell,-2)[/latex]) and solving the resulting two equations simultaneously gives: [latex]h=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}[/latex] So the rectangle's area is: [latex]\text{Area}=PL\times LM=\sqrt{\ell^2+4}\times\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{\ell^2+4}}=4[/latex] Remarkably, this is independent of [latex]\ell[/latex] — the area comes out to exactly [latex]4[/latex] regardless of where [latex]L[/latex] sits on [latex]QR[/latex], as long as [latex]MN[/latex] passes through [latex]S[/latex]. Answer: 4 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460442/gate-cse-2025-set-2-ga-question-9#a_list)

question: Let [latex]p_1 [/latex] and [latex]p_2 [/latex] denote two arbitrary prime numbers. Which one of the following statements is correct for all values of [latex]p_1 [/latex] and [latex]p_2 [/latex]?
options: [latex]p_1 + p_2 [/latex] is not a prime number.
[latex]p_1 p_2 [/latex] is not a prime number.
explanation: [Question 17 Explanation: Test each claim against simple examples with actual primes: - "[latex]p_1+p_2[/latex] is not prime": counterexample [latex]p_1=2,p_2=3\Rightarrow5[/latex] (prime!). False in general. - "[latex]p_1p_2[/latex] is not prime" : since both [latex]p_1[/latex] and [latex]p_2[/latex] are themselves prime (each [latex]\ge2[/latex]), their product always has at least two prime factors when counted with multiplicity — even if [latex]p_1=p_2[/latex], the product [latex]p_1^2[/latex] is still composite (divisible by [latex]p_1[/latex], which is neither [latex]1[/latex] nor the product itself). So the product can never be prime. Always true. - "[latex]p_1+p_2+1[/latex] is prime": counterexample [latex]p_1=2,p_2=3\Rightarrow6[/latex] (not prime). False in general. - "[latex]p_1p_2+1[/latex] is prime": counterexample [latex]p_1=3,p_2=5\Rightarrow16[/latex] (not prime). False in general. Answer: p1p2 is not a prime number. question: If [latex]Pe^{x} = Q e^{-x} [/latex] for all real values of [latex]x [/latex], which one of the following statements is true?
explanation: [Question 18 Explanation: [latex]Pe^x=Qe^{-x}[/latex] for every real [latex]x[/latex]. Multiply both sides by [latex]e^x[/latex]: [latex]Pe^{2x}=Q[/latex]. Since [latex]e^{2x}[/latex] genuinely varies with [latex]x[/latex] (it's not constant), the only way the left side can stay equal to the constant [latex]Q[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex] is if the coefficient [latex]P[/latex] itself is [latex]0[/latex]. With [latex]P=0[/latex], the equation becomes [latex]0=Q[/latex], so [latex]Q=0[/latex] too. Checking directly at [latex]x=0[/latex]: [latex]P=Q[/latex]. Combined with the "must hold for all [latex]x[/latex]" requirement, [latex]P=Q=0[/latex] is the only consistent solution. Answer: P = Q = 0 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460448/gate-cse-2025-set-2-ga-question-3#a_list)
